children.text: The answer: plenty. Just not everything.
Pyramids, GEM,
Luxor
, the
Valley of the Kings
, Karnak,
Aswan
, Philae, the Nile. Put this together properly and you have a strong first trip to Egypt. Try to add
Alexandria
, the White Desert, the Red Sea, Siwa,
Abu Simbel
, Dendera, and Abydos into the same week, and the trip breaks immediately.
Egypt is a country of distance.
Cairo

to Luxor is about 670 km. Luxor to Aswan is another 215 km further south. The transfers weigh more than the map suggests. So in a seven-day trip, what matters is not what to include but what to leave out.
For a first trip, the most stable answer is one shape.
Start in Cairo and
Giza
, fly to Aswan, move north along the Nile to Luxor, fly back to Cairo. That is the most practical way to see Egypt's spine in
seven days
The centre of a seven-day trip
For a first week, narrow the centre to three.
Cairo and Giza: pyramids, the Sphinx, the Grand Egyptian Museum, and as needed the city museums or old quarters.
Aswan: the light of the southern Nile, the
Philae temple
, Nubian culture, the post-High-Dam geography. Gentler than Luxor, and easy to settle into the trip's rhythm on arrival.
Luxor: the archaeological centre of the trip. Karnak,
Luxor Temple
, the Valley of the Kings, the Hatshepsut mortuary temple, the west-bank necropolis. To take Egypt's temples and tombs seriously, you cannot treat Luxor thinly.

To do these three properly in seven days, domestic flights are practical. The overnight train has its romance, but on a short itinerary it costs stamina and time. For travellers who want the sleeper as an experience, it is an option; for content priority on a first week, flying is stronger.
Model itinerary
This is the seven days easiest to recommend to a first traveller.
Day 1: arrive in Cairo
Don't be greedy on day one.
Diving straight into
Khan el-Khalili
or the pyramids after a long flight makes Cairo's intensity arrive first. Move from the airport to the hotel, drop bags, sort exchange and SIM, head out lightly in the evening. That is enough.

Choose the hotel by trip shape. For the plateau the next morning, a Giza stay is easier. To move all of Cairo, Zamalek, Garden City, or the Nile side is workable. With only seven days, hotel location is not atmosphere — it is transfer time itself.
Day 2:
the Giza plateau
and the GEM
Morning is the plateau.

Enter as early as possible. To see Khufu, Khafre, Menkaure, the Sphinx, the valley temple, and the topography, the cool morning is best. Entering the Great Pyramid requires a separate ticket and stamina. People uncomfortable in tight spaces or sensitive to heat don't need to push it.

Afternoon at the Grand Egyptian Museum. Sitting near the plateau, the GEM fills in context the pyramids alone don't show — the Tutankhamun collection, Khufu's boat, large-scale ancient Egypt displays.
This is a heavy day. Pairing pyramids and the GEM means lunch and breaks must be real. The GEM is not a museum for a tag-along hour. Give it at least half a day.
Day 3: fly to Aswan, Philae
Morning flight to Aswan.

Aswan moves at a different speed from Cairo or Luxor. The Nile is wide, the islands are many, granite and sand line the banks. The presence of Nubian culture appears in colour, music, house decoration, and language.

Afternoon, Philae. Dedicated to Isis and now relocated to Agilkia Island. The original Philae Island faced danger from dam construction and water-level change, and the temple was moved stone by stone through an international rescue. Including the boat crossing, it is a particularly Aswan visit.
With time, you can add the High Dam or
the Unfinished Obelisk
. Don't pack the transfer-day afternoon. Aswan rewards a little pause beside the Nile.
Day 4: deepen Aswan, or go to Abu Simbel
Two choices.
One: deepen Aswan.
The Nubian Museum
Elephantine Island

, the Nilometer, a Nubian village, a felucca or small boat on the Nile. The trip gains daily life and southern Egyptian context. Even for a first trip, it keeps you from ending on temples and tombs only.

Two: Abu Simbel as a day trip. The Great Temple of Ramses II and the smaller temple of Nefertari are among Egypt's strongest sites. Far from Aswan, with an early-morning start and a long day. Worth including on a seven-day trip; it costs stamina and sleep.
Which is correct depends on the trip. For monumental force, Abu Simbel. To feel Aswan itself, the town and islands. Doing both completely on a short trip leaves fatigue for Luxor.
Day 5: north along the Nile to Luxor
Move from Aswan to Luxor.
Methods vary. The most efficient is north by car or train. You can include Kom Ombo and Edfu on the way. With a Nile cruise, the whole itinerary has to fit the boat's sailing schedule.

Kom Ombo is the double temple dedicated to Sobek and Haroeris. Right beside the Nile, its symmetric architecture reads clearly. Edfu's Temple of Horus is famous for preservation. A Ptolemaic-period temple, very useful for understanding ancient Egyptian temple structure.

Whether you make this a pure transfer day or add the sites changes the density. With stamina, including Kom Ombo and Edfu earns its place. With fatigue, heading straight to Luxor and keeping the evening light helps the next day's west bank.
Day 6: the Luxor west and east banks
The most important day of the seven.

Morning starts at the Valley of the Kings. As early as possible. Beyond the standard ticket, consider Seti I, Ramses V and VI, and Tutankhamun on supplementary tickets. You don't need to enter every one. Tombs are quality over count. To read the walls and texts even a little, a good guide is highly valuable here.

Then the Hatshepsut mortuary temple. The three terraces set against the cliff carry an architectural force completely different from the underground tombs. With time, add Medinet Habu — Ramses III's temple, with colour and structure well preserved and crowds relatively gentle. It deepens the west bank.

Afternoon back to the east bank for Karnak or Luxor Temple. Ideally both; in one day it's heavy. Karnak wants half a day on its own; in seven days you have to compromise. Luxor Temple in the evening feels alive inside the modern town — easy to remember on a short trip.
Better to see the Valley of the Kings and one large temple well than to run everything. Luxor is not a one-day place. Knowing that is itself part of the trip's result.
Day 7: back to Cairo, departure
To match the international flight, fly back to Cairo in the morning.
For an evening departure, you can use a short Cairo window. The Egyptian Museum, NMEC, Coptic Cairo, Islamic Cairo, or hotel rest before the airport. The choice depends on stamina and flight time.

Don't put a big site or long transfer on the last day. Cairo traffic is unpredictable, and a domestic-to-international connection wants margin. A seven-day trip ends better with a little space than with a final cram.
A dahabiya-style seven days
For a quieter trip, build around a dahabiya.

A dahabiya is a small Nile sailing boat. Fewer passengers than a large cruise, slower pace, sometimes including stops like Elkab and Gebel el-Silsila that large ships skip. It suits a traveller who wants the Nile not as transit but as the trip's centre.
To include a dahabiya in seven days, shorten Cairo. For example: day 1 arrive Cairo, day 2 Giza and GEM, day 3 fly to Luxor and board, days 4–6 the Nile, day 7 from Aswan back to Cairo.

A beautiful choice for first travellers, with narrower overall scope. Cairo's city side, Alexandria, the Red Sea are out. River time is denser. Less "move around to see Egypt" and more "slow the speed and read."

Compared with a large cruise, a dahabiya's value is quiet, small group, mooring options, and closeness to the river — not facility flash. Quality varies by boat; confirm cabins, food, guide, Wi-Fi, safety equipment, and children's accommodations in advance.
Adding Alexandria
A seven-day trip with Alexandria is possible. Something has to come out.
Alexandria carries air different from pharaonic Egypt. Mediterranean, port, Hellenistic, Roman, modern cosmopolitan memory. A different kind of city from Cairo or Luxor.
You can day-trip; on a first seven-day trip it gets busy. To include it, give a Cairo day to it — the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, the catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa, the Qaitbay Fortress, a seaside lunch.

That day is taken from Cairo and Giza depth. For a first trip with strong priorities on the pyramids, GEM, Luxor, and Aswan, Alexandria can wait. For travellers who want Mediterranean Egypt alongside ancient Egypt, it earns its day.
There is no single right answer in seven days. Once you choose, don't grieve too much over what you cut.
What not to add
Don't force the Red Sea into seven days.

Hurghada, Sharm el-Sheikh, Marsa Alam each have value. Diving, snorkelling, beach, desert resort time. Adding the Red Sea on top of Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan makes transfers dominate. A single Red Sea night doesn't bring out the sea.

Same for the White Desert. A strong place; to do it properly it wants time, permission, a vehicle, and overnight desert prep. Forcing it into a first seven days means a big cut from southern Egypt or Cairo.
Siwa is the same. Too far. Siwa is a place that needs days on its own. Not a side addition to a one-week Egypt trip — the main destination of a different trip.
Abu Simbel is the exception you can consider. Far from Aswan, doable in a day. If you include it, give the surrounding days margin.
Where to use a guide
With a tight budget, choose where to use a guide.

Top priority is Luxor. The Valley of the Kings, Karnak, the Hatshepsut mortuary temple — without explanation the impression is there, but the meaning layers are largely lost. To read wall paintings, royal names, gods, the order of architecture, the religious axis, a good Egyptologist guide is needed.

Then Giza. Pyramids are so famous that the ground is full of simplified explanations and suspect stories. A good guide makes the plateau read not as three stone mountains but as a royal funerary complex.

In Aswan, guides earn their place at Philae and the Nubian Museum; the town itself can hold some free time. Walk the Nile, take a boat to an island, watch the late afternoon. Margin matters here, not only explanation.
The right expectations for seven days
A seven-day Egypt trip is not a completed form. It is a doorway.

Built well, it is a deep doorway. Pyramids show the Old Kingdom. The GEM shows the royal objects in new display context. Aswan shows the southern Nile's geography. Luxor shows the density of temples and tombs. Even in a short schedule, it becomes clear that Egypt is not a single era or a single landscape.
A failing seven days underestimates the country.
A succeeding seven days acknowledges the country's scale and draws one strong line.
Cairo and Giza. Aswan. Luxor.
Start from there.
Egypt is not a country that shows everything in the first week. It shows enough reasons to come back.

deck: An honest seven-day model for travellers with only a week — how to combine Cairo, Giza, Luxor, and Aswan.

seo.metaDescription: Explore Egypt's iconic sights and rich culture in just one week. Experience Egypt in 7 Days offers a perfect blend of adventure, history, and unforgettable memories.

title: Seven Days in Egypt
